proxy_input: My sister is entering engineering, but she's worried about fitting in with all the nerdy guys. Any tips for her to feel more comfortable?
target_output:
First, give your sister a huge congratulations! Engineering is a fantastic, challenging, and rewarding field, and she has already proven she has what it takes just by getting into the program. 

It is completely normal for her to feel intimidated by the stereotype of the "nerdy guy club." While engineering is still male-dominated, the culture is changing rapidly. Here are some practical tips to help her feel more comfortable, confident, and ready to thrive:

**1. Join the Society of Women Engineers (SWE)**
This is the number one thing she can do. Almost every university with an engineering program has a SWE chapter. It is an incredible way to instantly meet other women in her classes, find study buddies, get advice from upperclassmen, and realize she is not alone. 

**2. Reframe the "Nerdy Guy" Stereotype**
The media portrays engineering students as socially awkward guys who only care about video games and math. In reality, she will meet a huge variety of people. There will be college athletes, musicians, artists, and extroverts. As for the guys who *do* fit the "nerdy" stereotype—she'll likely find that many of them are incredibly kind, helpful, and just really passionate about how things work. Shared suffering over a difficult Calculus or Physics exam is a great equalizer and an easy way to make friends.

**3. She Doesn't Have to Change Who She Is**
Sometimes women in male-dominated fields feel the need to become "one of the guys" or hide their femininity to be taken seriously. She doesn't have to do that. She can love fashion, makeup, and pop culture, and still be the smartest person in her thermodynamics class. Authenticity commands respect.

**4. Take Charge of Group Work**
In engineering, there are a lot of group projects. Sometimes, unconscious bias means guys might try to relegate the female student to the "secretary" role (taking notes, making the PowerPoint). She should confidently volunteer for the technical tasks: *"I'll take the lead on the CAD model,"* or *"I'll write the code for this section."* 

**5. Form Study Groups Early**
She shouldn't wait for people to approach her. If she sits next to someone (guy or girl) who seems friendly, she should just say, *"A few of us are getting together at the library to work on this problem set, do you want to come?"* By being the initiator, she gets to build a circle of peers she actually likes and feels comfortable around.

**6. Prepare for Imposter Syndrome**
Many engineering students—especially women—experience imposter syndrome (the feeling that they tricked the admissions office and don't actually belong). Remind her that the classes are designed to be hard for *everyone*. If she struggles with a concept, it doesn't mean she isn't cut out for engineering; it just means she's learning. 

**7. Find Mentors**
She should look for female professors, teaching assistants (TAs), or junior/senior women in her major. Going to their office hours just to introduce herself and ask for advice on navigating the major can yield incredible support and future career connections.

**8. Remember Her "Why"**
When she feels out of place, she should remind herself why she chose engineering. Whether she wants to design sustainable energy solutions, build bridges, create medical devices, or just loves problem-solving, her perspective as a woman is desperately needed in the industry to design products that work for *everyone*.

Tell her to walk into her first day with her head held high. She earned her seat in that classroom just as much as anyone else!
